claim: The module docstring asserts the pool has exactly `SQL_WORKER_THREADS` workers all started on first use, that at most that many queries run at once, that further calls wait with no queue timeout, and that the saturation warning is logged at most once every `SATURATION_WARNING_INTERVAL_S` seconds.
source_excerpt:
- The pool has exactly :data:`SQL_WORKER_THREADS` worker threads, all started
  on first use, so at most that many queries run at once and a burst of slow
  queries holds no more than that many threads and database connections.
  Further calls wait in the pool's queue for as long as it takes; there is no
  queue timeout. When a call arrives while every worker is busy, a warning
  with the number of queued calls is logged, at most once every
  :data:`SATURATION_WARNING_INTERVAL_S` seconds.
verify_against: `_DaemonThreadPool.submit`, `_start_workers`, `_warn_saturated` and `_run` in the same file
verify_hint: Falsify with concurrent submits racing `submit`'s unlocked `len(self._threads)` check and with the `_busy` read taken before `self._work.put`: check `_DaemonThreadPool.submit` and `_warn_saturated`

claim: The module docstring asserts the workers never hold up process exit because they are daemon threads, and that `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` would instead join its workers at interpreter exit even after `shutdown(wait=False)`.
source_excerpt:
- The workers are daemon threads, so they never hold up process exit.
  ``concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`` is not used because it joins its
  workers when the interpreter exits, even after ``shutdown(wait=False)``: a
  query stuck in its driver would keep the process alive with no time limit.
verify_against: CPython's `threading._shutdown` / `concurrent.futures.thread` atexit handling
verify_hint: Check `concurrent.futures.thread._python_exit` and `threading._register_atexit` in the Python 3.11+ standard library, and whether any `threading._shutdown` path joins daemon threads

prior_evidence: Docstring part holds: probe_llm (src/sqllens/preflight.py:174-177) calls AnthropicLlmService with the same model/api_key args as factory.py:73-76, and the service applies env fallback for model/api_key/base_url (llm.py:61-63). Async construction needs no event loop and makes no request (llm.py:71). But docs/internal/setup/preflight.md:64 claims 'construction alone ... surfaces obviously-broken keys (the SDK rejects empty strings at construction)'. AnthropicLlmService only forwards the key when truthy (llm.py:66-67), so an empty-string key (e.g. SQLLENS_LLM__API_KEY='' giving SecretStr('')) is never passed to the SDK; it falls back to env or None, and the Anthropic SDK client does not reject a missing key at construction (it errors at request time; from SDK knowledge, SDK source not read here). So the empty-key case is not surfaced by probe_llm, and the doc claim is false for it.

claim: This finding from the previous review no longer holds at the reviewed head: 1. The new `_DaemonThreadPool` can lose track of which worker threads are idle, so `src/sqllens/agent/integrations/sql_threads.py` (lines 73-105) may run fewer concurrent queries than `SQL_WORKER_THREADS` allows. `submit` puts the work item on the queue and only then tests the `_idle` semaphore, while a worker releases its permit after its `get_nowait()` has already raised `queue.Empty`. In between, the worker can take the item the failed test caused a second worker to be spawned for, and then release a permit that stands for a thread that is already busy. A later `submit` consumes that stale permit, so it neither starts a worker nor logs, and its query waits in the queue behind a running one even though the pool is below its cap. That is the "a quick query waits behind a slow query" behavior the change sets out to remove, and it also makes `test_sql_pool_runs_at_most_its_worker_count_at_once` and `_fill_pool` in `tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py` nondeterministic. Nothing hangs permanently, because a queued item is always taken eventually. (raised by 4/6 agents)

A worker thread that fails to start leaves its work item queued, in `src/sqllens/agent/integrations/sql_threads.py` (lines 73-89). `submit` queues the item before calling `threading.Thread(...).start()`.
